purpose: Bring the chief information officer, chief information security officer, chief data officer, and chief AI officer perspectives into one accountable enterprise model.
staffSummary: Build M51 around one consequential utility situation and one decision: Assign decision rights, shared controls, operating ownership, architecture, assurance, and escalation for an enterprise AI portfolio. The learner must leave with a usable enterprise AI decision-rights and assurance charter, not a collection of definitions.
openingSituation: Technology, security, data, operations, legal, and innovation teams each believe another group owns the risk created by a growing set of AI tools.
learnerDecision: Assign decision rights, shared controls, operating ownership, architecture, assurance, and escalation for an enterprise AI portfolio.
analogy: A bridge needs structural, traffic, maintenance, safety, and owner perspectives. None can replace the others, and one authority must resolve the final decision.
learnerOutcomes: Explain The CIO, CISO, and Chief AI Officer: The Summit in plain English and connect it to a real water, wastewater, stormwater, or One Water decision.
Distinguish technology ownership, data ownership, security authority, AI governance, business ownership, assurance, and executive accountability without using one term to hide several different jobs.
Analyze the module situation, identify missing evidence, and name the professional consequence of a weak decision.
Compare how the same question changes across drinking water, wastewater, stormwater, administration, engineering, finance, technology, and public leadership.

Evaluate sources, assumptions, limitations, permissions, and human authority using this boundary: Do not create a chief AI officer title without decision rights, resources, controls, and operating relationships. Titles do not satisfy governance.
Create a usable enterprise AI decision-rights and assurance charter with evidence, roles, limits, review steps, and the next accountable action.
Defend the recommendation to Foundation, Practitioner, and Leader audiences while keeping disagreement and uncertainty visible.
curriculumOutcomes: Give The CIO, CISO, and Chief AI Officer: The Summit one clear learning job inside Role-Based Practice.
Connect the module to a consequential decision and the enterprise AI decision-rights and assurance charter.
Preserve current content, proposals, enhancements, and contributor records by stable identifier.
Separate verified evidence, Hardeep positions, expert interpretation, instructional scenarios, and unresolved questions.
Create an explicit bridge to the preceding and following modules without duplicating their work.
marketingOutcomes: Describe the practical value as helping a learner make and explain this decision: Assign decision rights, shared controls, operating ownership, architecture, assurance, and escalation for an enterprise AI portfolio.
Name the enterprise AI decision-rights and assurance charter as the visible result of the module.
Do not promise savings, compliance, certification, safety, performance, implementation success, or career outcomes without separately approved evidence.
requiredWorkProduct: enterprise AI decision-rights and assurance charter
definitionOfDone: The learner explains the core distinctions, completes the required evidence and decision activities, passes distributed checks, saves a complete enterprise AI decision-rights and assurance charter, and names the next accountable action.
scopeBoundary: Do not create a chief AI officer title without decision rights, resources, controls, and operating relationships. Titles do not satisfy governance.
researchQuestions: What must an intelligent newcomer understand about The CIO, CISO, and Chief AI Officer: The Summit before using it in utility work?
Which sources can support the distinctions among technology ownership, data ownership, security authority, AI governance, business ownership, assurance, and executive accountability?
What evidence would allow a practitioner to make this decision: Assign decision rights, shared controls, operating ownership, architecture, assurance, and escalation for an enterprise AI portfolio.
Which failure modes, counterexamples, and edge conditions could make the enterprise AI decision-rights and assurance charter misleading?
How does the question change across drinking water, wastewater, stormwater, reuse, finance, engineering, administration, technology, and public accountability?
Which actions require qualified operator, engineer, water-quality, cybersecurity, privacy, legal, procurement, records, finance, accessibility, or executive review?
Which claims remain outside the module boundary: Do not create a chief AI officer title without decision rights, resources, controls, and operating relationships. Titles do not satisfy governance.
